newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Gum arabic producers meet in Lagos on quality.
newsitem.headline: Gum arabic producers meet in Lagos on quality.

text.p: Producers of gum arabic, a vital raw material for industries found only in the semi-arid sahel belt of Africa, began a two-day seminar in Lagos on Wednesday to discuss how to improve the quality of the commodity.

"Export has been greatly hampered in the past by poor quality standards which in most cases arose from ignorance of producers on how best to achieve high quality," said Sa Ingawa, executive director of Nigeria's exports promotion council, one of the organisers of the seminar.
Participants include officials of exporting nations as well as buyers of the commodity.

"Due to wide scale adulteration, poor quality control practices and lack of adequate understanding of the market structure, gum arabic especially of Nigerian origin has faced tremendous difficulties in the international market," said Chidume Okoro, chairman of Tadecon, a major exporter Nigeria.
The seminar will be followed by a conference on Friday of the seven gum arabic producing nations at the end of which they expect to form an association to advance their interests.
The seven nations are Sudan, the biggest producer, Nigeria, Niger, Chad, Senegal, Mali and Mauritania.
Together they produce the estimated world output of 50,000 metric tonnes per annum shipped almost completely to developed countries for processing into industrial raw material.

The commodity, otherwise known as Acasia Senegalese after Senegal where it has its origin, is used widely in food, soft drink, pharmaceuticals, confectionery, textile, printing and cosmetics industries.
Most industries use it as a stabilising agent. While manufacturers of drugs use it to coat tablets, breweries and food firms use it as a preservative.
Nigeria is the second biggest producer with output of 5,000 tonnes and one billion naira ($12.5 million) income annually.
Ingawa said the seminar would also examine the emergence of starch as a substitute for gum arabic.
"This development, I must say could be a threat to the exportation of gum arabic," he said.
